chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Optimization Theory Matters for Portfolio Construction

lessons.title: What Is an Optimization Problem? Objective Functions, Variables, and Constraints

children.text: Ananya is three rounds into an interview process with a proprietary trading desk in Mumbai. The quant on the video call shares his screen: three stocks, their expected returns, and a 3x3 covariance matrix. Find the portfolio weights that minimize risk, he says, given that the weights must add up to one. Ananya has Excel open. She could set up Solver and let it grind toward an answer, but the interviewer follows up immediately: now do it without Solver, on paper, and tell me why your answer is the minimum and not just a number a spreadsheet spat out. She has no answer. This is the gap this course exists to close: not just building portfolios, but proving mathematically that the weights you chose are actually optimal, not merely plausible.

body.text: Every optimization problem, no matter how complicated it looks, is built from exactly three ingredients: what you are allowed to change, what you are trying to make as small or as large as possible, and the rules you are not allowed to break. Portfolio construction is optimization wearing a finance costume.

children.text: The Three Ingredients of Every Optimization Problem

markDefs.definition: The quantities you are actually free to choose in a problem. In portfolio construction, these are almost always the portfolio weights: how much of your capital goes into each asset.

The single number, built from the decision variables, that you are trying to make as small or as large as possible. In portfolio construction, this is usually risk (to minimize) or expected return (to maximize).

The rules the decision variables must obey, no matter how good breaking them would make the objective function look. Example: portfolio weights must add up to 1, or no single stock can exceed 30% of the portfolio.

children.text: Strip away the finance vocabulary and an optimization problem is three things bolted together. First, the
decision variables
. Second, the
objective function
. Third, the
constraints
. Every model in this course, from a two-stock minimum variance portfolio to a KKT-constrained, long-only Nifty 50 portfolio, is these same three ingredients written with different numbers.
A Concrete Example: The Minimum Variance Portfolio

Take the exact problem Ananya's interviewer posed. She has three stocks, say Reliance Industries, TCS, and HDFC Bank, and needs to decide how much weight to put on each so the resulting portfolio has the lowest possible variance, while investing the full amount available: no cash left idle, no leverage.

body.caption: The objective function: minimize portfolio variance, where w is the vector of weights and Sigma is the covariance matrix of returns.
The constraint: every rupee gets allocated. None held back, none borrowed.

children.text: If you have already worked through portfolio variance for two assets, you know wᵀΣw expands into weighted individual variances plus a cross term for covariance. Nothing new is happening mathematically here. It is the same variance formula, compressed into a single matrix expression so it generalizes cleanly from three stocks to thirty, or three hundred, without the algebra getting any longer to write down.
Minimize or Maximize? It's the Same Machinery

Ananya's problem minimizes risk. A different, equally common problem maximizes expected return for the same three stocks, subject to the same budget rule. Both are optimization problems built from identical ingredients, just pointed in different directions.

cells: Constraint: w1 + w2 + w3 = 1 (often plus a variance cap)

body.label: Maximizing f(x)
body.context: Same optimal decision variables either way. This is why every method this course builds, from Lagrange multipliers to KKT conditions, works for both risk-minimizing and return-maximizing portfolios without needing separate machinery.

body.text: Notice that stating the problem this way does not solve it. Excel Solver could numerically grind toward an answer for Ananya's three stocks, but it cannot tell you why that answer is optimal, or how the optimal weights shift if the covariance matrix changes next quarter. That is exactly the gap Lagrange multipliers close, starting in Chapter 4, and what KKT conditions extend to handle real constraints like no short-selling in Chapter 5.

children.text: Why Not Just Guess, or Let a Solver Handle It?

body.title: Numerical Solver vs Solving It Analytically

columns.label: Guessing / Spreadsheet Solver
points: Fast for one specific dataset, one specific run
Gives you a number, not a reason it is optimal
Breaks silently if a new constraint is entered wrong
Tells you nothing about how the answer would change if inputs shift

columns.label: Solving It Analytically (this course)
points: Proves the solution is genuinely optimal, not just plausible
Shows exactly how the optimal weights move when inputs change
Scales from 3 stocks to 300 without rebuilding the logic
Is what quantitative interviews and real portfolio systems actually test for

children.text: The Feasible Region: Where the Rules Let You Stand

markDefs.definition: The set of every decision variable combination that satisfies all constraints simultaneously. The optimal solution, if one exists, lies inside this region or on its boundary.

children.text: Every combination of weights that satisfies all your constraints together forms what is called the
feasible region

. For Ananya's problem, that is every (w1, w2, w3) triple adding up to exactly 1, including negative weights unless she adds a no-short-selling rule. Somewhere inside or on the boundary of that region sits the one combination that also minimizes portfolio variance. The machinery this course builds, gradients in Chapter 3, Lagrange multipliers in Chapter 4, KKT conditions in Chapter 5, exists to find that one point without checking every other point in the region.

The rest of Chapter 1 connects this vocabulary directly to the Markowitz framework you may already know. Chapter 2 then introduces the one property, convexity, that guarantees this kind of problem can actually be solved instead of just described.

body.title: Name the decision variables
body.question: A quant wants to build a portfolio of 5 Nifty 50 stocks that maximizes expected return, subject to the total invested capital equaling ₹10 lakh exactly and no single stock exceeding 30% of the portfolio. What are the decision variables?
options: The expected returns of the 5 stocks
The covariance matrix of the 5 stocks
The portfolio weights (or rupee amounts) assigned to each of the 5 stocks
The level of the Nifty 50 index
body.explanation: Decision variables are what you are free to choose. Expected returns and the covariance matrix are inputs estimated from historical data, not choices. The weights, or equivalently the rupee amounts allocated to each stock, are the only things actually being decided here.

body.title: Fill in the term
body.textWithBlank: The set of all decision variable combinations that satisfy every constraint at once is called the ___.
body.explanation: The feasible region is the space you are allowed to search in. The optimal solution, if one exists, lies inside it or on its boundary, never outside it.

cards.definition: The quantities you are free to choose, such as portfolio weights.
The single number built from the decision variables that you are trying to minimize or maximize, such as portfolio variance or expected return.
The rules the decision variables must satisfy, such as weights summing to 1 or no short-selling.
The set of all decision variable combinations that satisfy every constraint simultaneously.
The point within the feasible region where the objective function reaches its best, minimum or maximum, value.

points: Every optimization problem, however complex, reduces to three ingredients: decision variables, an objective function, and constraints.
In portfolio construction, the decision variables are almost always the portfolio weights.
Minimizing risk and maximizing return are the same kind of problem; maximizing f(x) is identical to minimizing -f(x).
The feasible region is every combination of weights that satisfies your constraints. The optimal solution sits inside it or on its boundary.
Spreadsheet solvers can find a numerical answer but cannot prove it is optimal or show how it moves when inputs change. That is what the rest of this course builds toward.
